name: Tokyo
tagline: Neon canyons, silent shrines and the world's best bowl of noodles
description:
Tokyo is less a single city than a federation of villages that happen to share a train network. Step off at Shibuya and you are swept into a scramble of screens and sneaker shops; ride twenty minutes to Yanaka and you find cats dozing on temple walls, tofu sellers and wooden houses that survived both the 1923 earthquake and the war. The genius of the place is how smoothly it switches registers, from hushed cedar forest to eight-story arcade, without ever feeling chaotic.

Food is the obvious reason to come and the hardest to over-hype. The city holds more Michelin stars than anywhere else on earth, yet the most memorable meals often cost under ten dollars: a counter bowl of shoyu ramen at midnight, a convenience-store egg sandwich at dawn, skewers of chicken grilled over white charcoal beneath a railway arch.

Practically, Tokyo is a dream for first-timers. Trains run to the second, streets are spotless, lost wallets come back, and nearly everything is signposted in English. Come in late March for cherry blossoms or November for fiery maples, pack comfortable shoes, and leave room in your schedule simply to wander.

safety.notes: Violent crime is extremely rare and walking alone at night is generally fine. In Kabukichō and Roppongi, ignore street touts and never follow a promoter into a bar, where inflated bills and drink-spiking have been reported.

tipping: Tipping is not practiced and can cause confusion, since good service is simply part of the price; a small envelope for a private guide is the rare exception.
gettingAround: Add a Suica or PASMO card to your phone (or buy a Welcome Suica at the airport) and ride the JR Yamanote loop plus Tokyo Metro, which reach nearly every sight. Trains stop around midnight, so budget for a taxi if you stay out late.
tips: Konbini food is genuinely good: an egg sandwich, onigiri and a canned coffee make a perfect $5 breakfast, and 7-Eleven ATMs reliably accept foreign cards.
Many small restaurants, shrines and older shops are still cash-only, so keep ¥10,000–20,000 on you even if you mostly pay by card.
Queue for famous ramen or tonkatsu spots around 11:00 or after 14:00; the noon-to-13:00 office rush can easily double your wait.
Send big suitcases ahead with a hotel-desk luggage forwarding service (takkyūbin) for about $15–25 a bag and ride the trains with just a daypack.
Rush hour on the Yamanote, Chūō and Tōzai lines (roughly 07:30–09:30) is famously crushing, so start museum days at 10:00 instead.
Most museums close on Mondays; check hours before planning a Monday culture day, and use it for markets, shrines and neighborhoods instead.
etiquette: Avoid eating while walking along busy streets; stand beside the stall or vending machine to finish your snack.
Keep your phone on silent and skip calls on trains, and talk quietly in carriages.
Take off your shoes where you see a raised step or slippers at the entrance, and never wear the toilet slippers back into the room.
At shrines, bow once at the torii gate, rinse your hands at the water basin and avoid walking down the exact center of the path, which is reserved for the deities.

neighborhoods.name: Shinjuku
neighborhoods.blurb: Skyscraper offices, the world's busiest station, the smoky yakitori lanes of Omoide Yokochō and the tiny bars of Golden Gai, all within a ten-minute walk.

neighborhoods.name: Shibuya
neighborhoods.blurb: Youth-culture central: the famous scramble crossing, rooftop views, vintage shops in Ura-Harajuku and cocktail bars tucked into the backstreets.

neighborhoods.name: Asakusa
neighborhoods.blurb: Old-Edo atmosphere around Sensō-ji, with rickshaw pullers, craft shops and cheap riverside izakaya, plus Skytree just across the Sumida.

neighborhoods.name: Yanaka
neighborhoods.blurb: A slice of prewar Tokyo with temple cemeteries, cat-themed shops and the sleepy Yanaka Ginza shopping street, a short walk from Ueno's museums.

neighborhoods.name: Shimokitazawa
neighborhoods.blurb: A bohemian maze of vintage clothing, record stores, micro-theaters and third-wave coffee, now threaded with a leafy park along the old rail line.

dishes.name: Edomae sushi
dishes.description: Nigiri the way Tokyo invented it, with fish lightly cured, soy-marinated or simmered before meeting warm, red-vinegar rice; it began as fast food on the stalls of old Edo.

dishes.name: Shoyu ramen
dishes.description: Clear, soy-seasoned chicken broth with springy curly noodles, bamboo shoots and chashu pork; the capital's classic style and the perfect 1 a.m. meal.

dishes.name: Monjayaki
dishes.description: A runny batter of cabbage, spicy cod roe and cheese fried on a tabletop griddle and scraped up with tiny spatulas; Tsukishima is its spiritual home.

dishes.name: Tendon
dishes.description: A bowl of rice crowned with crisp shrimp and vegetable tempura and drenched in sweet-savory sauce, a specialty of old Asakusa shops.

dishes.name: Chanko nabe
dishes.description: The protein-packed hotpot that fuels sumo wrestlers, best eaten in Ryōgoku near the national sumo arena.

events.name: Hanami (Cherry Blossom Season)
events.description: From late March into early April, Ueno Park, Shinjuku Gyoen and the Meguro River fill with picnic blankets and lantern-lit night viewings; bloom forecasts are published weeks ahead.

events.name: Sanja Matsuri
events.description: On the third weekend of May, Asakusa erupts as teams in happi coats bounce more than 100 portable shrines through the streets around Sensō-ji.

events.name: Sumida River Fireworks Festival
events.description: On the last Saturday of July around 20,000 fireworks light up the sky over the Sumida River; locals stake out riverbank spots by early afternoon.

events.name: Tori-no-Ichi
events.description: On the 'rooster days' of November, Ōtori shrines host night fairs selling ornate bamboo rakes meant to rake in good fortune, sealed with rhythmic hand-clapping.

attractions.name: Sensō-ji
attractions.description: Tokyo's oldest temple is reached through the thunderous red Kaminarimon gate and a long gauntlet of snack and souvenir stalls on Nakamise-dōri. Come at dawn or after dark, when the crowds thin, the five-story pagoda glows under floodlights and you can draw an omikuji fortune in peace.
attractions.bookingTip: No tickets needed; arrive before 08:00 to photograph Kaminarimon without a wall of selfie sticks.

attractions.name: Meiji Shrine
attractions.description: A towering cypress torii leads into 70 hectares of hand-planted forest where the din of Harajuku vanishes within a hundred steps. Look for the wall of donated sake barrels, write a wish on a wooden ema plaque, and on weekends you may glimpse a traditional wedding procession under red parasols.
attractions.hours: Sunrise to sunset daily (roughly 05:00–18:00, varies by month)
attractions.bookingTip: Enter from Harajuku Station and leave through the north gate toward Yoyogi to pair a forest walk with Omotesandō's cafés.

attractions.name: Shibuya Crossing
attractions.description: Up to 3,000 people surge across this multi-way scramble every time the lights change, beneath a canyon of giant video screens. Watch it first from above, from the Shibuya Sky rooftop or a second-floor café window, then dive in yourself, ideally on a rainy night when the umbrellas turn it into moving art.
attractions.bookingTip: If you want the rooftop view, book a Shibuya Sky sunset slot online several days ahead, as those sell out first.

attractions.name: Tokyo Skytree
attractions.description: At 634 meters this is the tallest tower in the world, and its glass spiral ramp at 450 meters looks down on an endless grid of rooftops, with Mount Fuji floating on the horizon on crisp winter mornings. The mall at its base is handy for rainy-day souvenir shopping and a surprisingly good food floor.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy a timed ticket online to skip the queue, and check the weather in the morning, since haze can hide Fuji by midday.

attractions.name: Tokyo National Museum
attractions.description: Japan's oldest and largest museum sits at the top of Ueno Park and holds samurai armor, lacquered Buddhas, ukiyo-e prints and nearly 90 National Treasures, rotated so no two visits are the same. The Gallery of Hōryū-ji Treasures, a serene modernist box of gilt-bronze statues, is often almost empty.
attractions.bookingTip: General admission rarely sells out, but blockbuster special exhibitions need a timed ticket booked online.

attractions.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
attractions.description: The wholesale tuna auctions moved to Toyosu in 2018, but the maze of 400-odd shops and stalls around the old site stayed put and still supplies chefs across the city. Graze on sweet rolled omelette on a stick, butter-soy grilled scallops and fresh sea urchin, then browse knife shops that will engrave your purchase while you wait.
attractions.hours: Most stalls 07:00–14:00; many closed Sun, Wed and holidays
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive by 08:00 on a weekday; by late morning the lanes are shoulder to shoulder and the best stalls sell out.

attractions.name: Shinjuku Gyoen
attractions.description: Once an imperial retreat, this 58-hectare park stitches together a formal French garden, a sweeping English lawn and a Japanese landscape garden with teahouses and koi ponds. Alcohol is banned, which makes it the city's most civilized cherry-blossom spot, and the tropical greenhouse is a cozy refuge on a cold day.
attractions.hours: 09:00–16:00 (later in spring and summer), closed Mon
attractions.bookingTip: In cherry-blossom season arrive right at opening; by late morning the gate queues can stretch past 30 minutes.

attractions.name: Ghibli Museum
attractions.description: Hayao Miyazaki's whimsical museum on the edge of Inokashira Park feels like walking into one of his films, with spiral staircases, hidden doors and a giant robot soldier standing guard on the rooftop garden. Every ticket includes a short animated film that is screened nowhere else in the world.
attractions.bookingTip: Timed tickets go on sale on the 10th of the preceding month and sell out within hours; there are no tickets at the door.

attractions.name: Tokyo Imperial Palace
attractions.description: The emperor's residence hides behind massive stone walls and moats on the site of the shoguns' Edo Castle. Free guided walks cross the inner grounds, while the East Gardens let you climb the old keep's foundations among plum, iris and azalea beds, and joggers circle the 5-kilometer moat loop from dawn.
attractions.hours: East Gardens 09:00–16:00 (later in summer), closed Mon and Fri
attractions.bookingTip: Reserve the free palace grounds tour online in advance, or join the same-day registration queue at Kikyō-mon gate before it opens.

attractions.name: Golden Gai
attractions.description: Six narrow alleys hold roughly 200 bars, most barely wider than a closet and seating six or eight people on creaky stools. Each has its own obsession, from punk records to horror films, and wandering until a bartender waves you in is the whole point.
attractions.bookingTip: Expect a ¥500–1,500 seating charge per bar, look for English or 'welcome' signs on the door, and never photograph inside without asking.

hotels.name: Ōtemon Pavilion
hotels.description: Floors 30 to 38 of a Marunouchi tower frame the palace moats and, on clear winter mornings, Mount Fuji. Rooms pair hinoki-wood soaking tubs with washi paper screens, and the spa's mineral water is trucked in from Hakone hot springs.

hotels.name: Kaminari Lantern Inn
hotels.description: A former kimono wholesaler's warehouse turned 22-room inn, three minutes from Kaminarimon. Rooms mix tatami platforms with proper beds, and the rooftop deck frames a glowing Skytree above the temple roofs at night.

hotels.name: Scramble Loft Hotel
hotels.description: Concrete, walnut and a vinyl turntable in every room: this design hotel above a Dōgenzaka record shop was built for night owls. The 12th-floor bar looks straight down onto the crossing and pours Japanese whisky flights until 2 a.m.

hotels.name: Yanaka Cat & Cedar Hostel
hotels.description: A creaky 1950s wooden house with curtained bunk pods, a shared kitchen and an elderly resident cat named Daifuku. Staff lead free morning walks through Yanaka's temple lanes, and Ueno's museums are a 12-minute stroll away.

hotels.name: Gyoen Garden Ryokan
hotels.description: Tucked down a lane beside the garden's Ōkido Gate, this 14-room ryokan serves seasonal kaiseki dinners in your room and runs cedar-scented communal baths. It is a startling pocket of calm ten minutes from Shinjuku's neon.

hotels.name: Tsukishima Canal Apartments
hotels.description: Compact one- and two-bedroom apartments with washer-dryers and full kitchens, just across the Kachidoki Bridge from Tsukiji. Great for families or longer stays, with Tsukishima's monjayaki street two minutes from the door.

restaurants.name: Kōshi Tendon
restaurants.description: A ten-seat counter where the third-generation chef fries shrimp, conger eel and seasonal vegetables in sesame oil until they shatter. The dark, sweet sauce is ladled on at the last second; expect a short queue at lunch and a very contented nap afterward.
restaurants.signatureDish: Edomae tendon with conger eel and kakiage

restaurants.name: Kawasemi Sushi
restaurants.description: Tucked above a knife shop in the outer market, this 12-seat counter serves a 15-piece lunch omakase built on whatever the buyer brought back from Toyosu that morning. Aged tuna, kelp-cured sea bream and warm red-vinegar rice give it a depth usually found at places costing three times as much.
restaurants.signatureDish: Omakase nigiri with aged bluefin tuna

restaurants.name: Ramen Kitsunebi
restaurants.description: A ticket-machine ramen shop on the edge of Golden Gai that simmers a clear, soy-sharp chicken and dried-sardine broth all day. It stays open until 5 a.m., which makes it the traditional last stop after a bar crawl.
restaurants.signatureDish: Shoyu ramen with niboshi sardine broth

restaurants.name: Kissa Hoshizora
restaurants.description: An unrestored 1970s coffee house with velvet booths, siphon brewers and a jazz record always spinning. The 'morning set' of thick buttered toast, a boiled egg and hand-brewed coffee is served until 11:00 for under $6.
restaurants.signatureDish: Thick-cut toast morning set with siphon coffee

restaurants.name: Tsuyukusa
restaurants.description: An eight-seat kaiseki counter on the 20th floor overlooking the palace moats, where each of the 11 courses tracks a micro-season of the old lunar calendar. Expect charcoal-grilled sweetfish in summer, matsutake broth in autumn and a sake pairing drawn from tiny rural breweries.
restaurants.signatureDish: Seasonal hassun platter and clay-pot rice

restaurants.name: Midori-no-Mori Shōjin
restaurants.description: Temple-style vegan cooking served in lacquered boxes a few minutes from the shrine's south gate. Sesame tofu, simmered freeze-dried tofu and crisp vegetable tempura prove that meatless Japanese food can be deeply satisfying.

restaurants.name: Osteria Sanpo
restaurants.description: A cheerful Italian kitchen with a wood-fired oven on the lane between Inokashira Park and the museum. The chef trained in Bologna and rolls tagliatelle daily, but Japanese touches like whitebait-and-yuzu pizza are what keep regulars coming back.

restaurants.name: Izakaya Kawazoi
restaurants.description: A lantern-hung izakaya on a canal a few minutes from Skytree, loved by locals for its cheap highballs and handwritten menu of grilled fish, chicken-skin gyoza and potato salad with smoked egg. Staff will happily let you point at whatever the next table is eating.

experiences.name: Lantern Alleys Night Food Crawl
experiences.description: A local host leads six travelers through Omoide Yokochō's smoky yakitori stalls, a standing sake bar and two tiny Golden Gai hideaways, ordering the things you would never find alone. Expect chicken hearts, pickled-plum highballs and stories of postwar Shinjuku.

experiences.name: Asakusa Kimono Stroll & Tea Ceremony
experiences.description: A professional dresser fits you in a seasonal kimono, then a tea master teaches you to whisk matcha and eat wagashi properly in a tatami room behind the temple. The kimono is yours for the rest of the session to wander Sensō-ji's lanes.

experiences.name: Hakone Hot Springs & Fuji Views Day Trip
experiences.description: Meet in Marunouchi for a day of lake cruising, steaming volcanic valleys and eggs blackened in sulfur vents, with Mount Fuji views when the clouds cooperate. The day ends with a long soak at a traditional onsen before the train back to the city.

experiences.name: Sumida River Twilight Yakatabune Cruise
experiences.description: Board a low-roofed yakatabune boat near Skytree and glide down the Sumida under illuminated bridges to Tokyo Bay while a chef fries tempura on board. Sit on tatami, drink freely and climb to the roof deck for Rainbow Bridge views.
